name: Nyangumarta
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: In Nyangumarta the following generalisations can be made about stress placement: (2.66) a. Primary stress occurs on the initial syllable of a word and there is stress on alternating syllalbes. b. Stress occurs on the first syllable of reduplicated roots. c. Stress occurs on the initial syllable of bisyllabic and polysyllabic nominal suffixes. d. The final syllable of a word does not bear stress. e. Monosyllabic verb roots are stressed. f. Verbalisers of one or two syllables bear stress on the first syllable. g. Primary stress occurs on the first word of a phonological phrase and secondary stress occurs on the second word of a phonological phrase and each successive phonological word in the phrase
new_statements.citation: Sharp, Janet. 2004. Nyangumarta: a language of the Pilbara region of Western Australia (Pacific Linguistics 556). Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, RSPAS, ANU.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the initial syllable; secondary stresses fall on alternating syllables thereafter, but never on the word-final syllable; polysyllabic suffixes, verbalisers and each reduplicand restart stress on their own first syllable (morphologically sensitive rhythm). Ch.3 p.98 restates: 'Nyangumarta words (either simple or complex) carry main stress on the first syllable'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stress on alternating syllables after the initial; bisyllabic/polysyllabic nominal suffixes and one/two-syllable verbalisers take stress on their first syllable; both halves of reduplicated roots stressed; within a phonological phrase the first phonological word has primary stress and each following phonological word secondary stress (§2.5, §2.6g); verbal pronoun word-forms take secondary stress on their first syllable (ch.3, Table 3.2 discussion).
new_statements.exceptions: Final syllable of a word never bears stress (2.66d); monosyllabic verb roots are stressed (2.66e); ch.3 notes secondary stress can also occur on the suffixes -yirni 1PL.EXC.SUB and -layi 1DU.EXC.SUB, and (p.~140 in text) for some speakers stress occurs on the second syllable of a particular suffix; -pi-RN consistently stressed in certain stative/inchoative constructions.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule (simple and complex words) plus a separate phonological-phrase rule (primary on first phonological word, secondary on subsequent words, one intonation contour). Description based predominantly on the southern inland dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: Sharp (2004:§1.3) states the description refers predominantly to the southern inland dialect of Nyangumarta (Wanyarli; spoken by the Strelley Mob, around Port/South Hedland and Marble Bar), with occasional reference to the northern coastal dialect (Ngurlipartu). Language-level glottocode nyan1301 applies.
